ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Cryptococcosis is an opportunistic infection caused by the encapsulated yeast Cryptococcus neoformans, often acquired from pigeon droppings or soil. It primarily affects immunocompromised patients, especially those with AIDS, and can cause meningitis or disseminated disease.

sections.p: Cryptococcus neoformans is a basidiomycetous yeast with a thick polysaccharide capsule that protects it from host defenses. Infection occurs after inhalation of aerosolised yeast, then spreads hematogenously, especially to the central nervous system.
b: Encapsulated yeast, 4–6 µm, reproduces by budding
Found in pigeon droppings, decaying wood, soil

sections.p: The capsule is the key virulence factor, preventing phagocytosis and dampening the immune response. The organism grows at 30‑37 °C and forms mucoid colonies on Sabouraud agar.
b: Polysaccharide capsule → positive India ink stain
Melanin production → protects against oxidative stress

sections.p: Inhalation of dried yeast cells or spores from contaminated environments initiates pulmonary infection. In immunocompetent hosts the disease is often subclinical; in immunocompromised hosts it disseminates.
b: No human‑to‑human transmission
Environmental reservoir: pigeon droppings, nitrogen‑rich soil

sections.p: Pulmonary cryptococcosis may present with cough or be silent. The most feared manifestation is cryptococcal meningitis, presenting with headache, fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. Disseminated disease can involve skin, bone, and blood.
b: Meningitis: most common in AIDS (CD4 < 100 cells/µL)
Pulmonary nodules or infiltrates
Skin lesions: papules, ulcers, cryptococcomas

sections.p: Laboratory confirmation relies on detecting the capsule or antigen, and culturing the organism. In low‑resource settings, India ink microscopy is often the first test.

t.b: Does the CSF show a clear halo around yeast? Positive indicates capsule presence; a negative result does not rule out disease.

t.a: Cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) latex agglutination or lateral flow assay
t.b: Is antigen detected in serum/CSF? Highly sensitive; a positive result confirms infection even if microscopy is negative.
Does the sample grow mucoid, cream‑coloured colonies? Confirms species; if culture unavailable, rely on antigen and microscopy.

sections.p: Induction therapy combines an azole (fluconazole) with flucytosine to rapidly reduce fungal burden, followed by consolidation and maintenance fluconazole. Management also includes managing intracranial pressure and immune reconstitution.
b: Fluconazole: fungistatic, penetrates CSF, low toxicity
Flucytosine: synergistic, rapid fungicidal effect; avoid if renal dysfunction
Control intracranial pressure: serial lumbar punctures

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams: capsule detection, CrAg test, association with AIDS, and the three‑phase treatment regimen.
b: India ink → capsule; CrAg → most sensitive test
Induction: fluconazole + flucytosine; then fluconazole alone
High mortality if meningitis untreated; monitor pressure

whenToSeekHelp: Acute headache, fever, neck stiffness, or altered consciousness (possible meningitis)
New skin lesions in an immunocompromised patient

faq.a: It blocks phagocytosis and interferes with complement, allowing the yeast to survive in the bloodstream.

faq.q: Can cryptococcosis occur in people with normal immunity?
faq.a: Yes, but it is usually mild or asymptomatic; severe disease is rare without immune compromise.

faq.q: What is the role of flucytosine in therapy?
faq.a: Flucytosine adds rapid fungicidal activity during induction; it is avoided if renal function is poor.
